description: Odysseus returns to Ithaca — the recognition scenes, the contest of the bow, and the slaughter of the suitors.
content_html:
The Return to Ithaca: Disguise and Deception

When Odysseus finally reaches Ithaca in Book 13, the goddess Athena disguises him as an old beggar. This disguise is essential to his plan: Ithaca is filled with over a hundred suitors who have taken over his palace, are consuming his wealth and are competing to marry his wife Penelope. If Odysseus is recognised too soon, he will be killed before he can prepare. The disguise is one of the most sustained and elaborate acts of deception in the poem, and it lasts through Books 13 to 22.

The theme of disguise and recognition is one of the Odyssey’s most powerful structural devices. Homer builds intense dramatic irony by allowing the audience to know what the characters in the poem do not: the ragged beggar shuffling through the halls of his own palace is the great king Odysseus. This gap between what the audience knows and what the suitors assume — that they are safe, that Odysseus is dead, that they may treat a helpless beggar with contempt — makes their eventual destruction feel both inevitable and just.

Book 19: Penelope and the Recognition by Eurycleia

In Book 19, still in his beggar’s disguise, Odysseus has a long, remarkable conversation with Penelope. She does not know she is speaking to her husband. She tells the “stranger” about her famous trick: she has been weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus’s father Laertes and has promised to choose a new husband when it is finished. Every night she unpicks the weaving she has done during the day, buying herself years of time. This deception is a mirror of Odysseus’s own resourcefulness — husband and wife are revealed to be perfectly matched in their use of cunning to protect what matters most to them.

The recognition scene that follows is both touching and tense. Penelope calls for the old nurse Eurycleia to wash the beggar’s feet — an act of hospitality appropriate for a guest. As Eurycleia washes his legs, her hands find a scar on his thigh. The poem pauses the action entirely to tell the story of how Odysseus received the scar as a young man, hunting a boar on Mount Parnassus with his grandfather Autolycus. This long digression — a retardation technique, not the anagnorisis itself — is a deliberate slowing of the pace that builds the dramatic tension almost unbearably. The anagnorisis comes immediately after: the moment Eurycleia’s hands find the scar and she realises the beggar is Odysseus.

Eurycleia gasps and looks up. Odysseus grabs her throat and silences her with a warning: no one must know. She agrees. This is the first human recognition in the palace, and it confirms for the audience what Odysseus has known all along — that there are loyal people in Ithaca waiting for his return, and that his plan can succeed.

Key Fact

Penelope’s weaving deception is her equivalent of Odysseus’s cunning: she weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unpicks it by night, delaying her choice of a husband for years. The parallel between husband and wife — both using deception to hold off those who would take what is theirs — is one of Homer’s most deliberate structural echoes.

Book 21: The Contest of the Bow

In Book 21, Penelope announces a contest to decide who she will marry: any man who can string Odysseus’s great bow and shoot an arrow through the sockets of twelve axe-heads in a row may have her hand. The great bow of Odysseus, given to him long ago by the hero Iphitus, is an object of enormous symbolic importance. It is kept under lock and key and has not been used since he left for Troy. To string it requires enormous strength and skill — the kind that only its owner possesses.

One by one, the suitors try and fail to string the bow. The wood is seasoned and stiff; the string requires a technique that none of them can master. The contest grinds to a humiliating halt. Then Odysseus, still in his beggar’s disguise, asks to be allowed to try. The suitors mock him furiously. Penelope supports his right to attempt it. Odysseus strings the bow with casual ease — “as a skilled musician strings a lyre,” as Homer says in one of his most elegant extended similes — and shoots cleanly through all twelve axe-heads without rising from his stool.

The homecoming books contrast loyal and disloyal servants carefully. The swineherd Eumaeus and the cowherd Philoetius remain loyal to Odysseus throughout: they refuse to side with the suitors, treat the disguised beggar with xenia, and are entrusted with a role in the final battle. Eurycleia recognises Odysseus and keeps his secret.

In contrast, twelve maidservants have slept with the suitors and sided against Penelope. The goatherd Melanthius has actively helped the suitors and insults Odysseus even when disguised. After the slaughter of the suitors, these disloyal servants are punished: the maidservants are forced to clean up the bodies before being hanged in the courtyard, and Melanthius is mutilated. The poem’s treatment of these characters reflects a worldview in which loyalty to a rightful lord is a supreme virtue, and its betrayal demands the harshest punishment.

Book 22: The Slaughter of the Suitors

The moment after Odysseus strings the bow is the pivot of the whole poem. He turns, shoots the leading suitor Antinous through the throat, and announces himself: “You thought I would never come home from Troy. You have been wasting my household, violating my maidservants, and seeking to take my wife while I still lived. Dogs — you never feared the gods who rule the spacious heaven, or the anger of men to come. Your day of reckoning has arrived.” The battle that follows is swift and brutal. Odysseus and three loyal helpers — his son Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius — kill all the suitors in the great hall.

The massacre is presented by Homer as an act of dike — justice — rather than mere revenge. The suitors have violated the sacred rules of xenia by abusing their host’s hospitality for years. They have dishonoured Penelope, threatened Telemachus and wasted Odysseus’s wealth. The gods, particularly Zeus, have sanctioned the punishment. Athena appears in the hall to tip the balance at a critical moment, showing that divine approval stamps the act as righteous.

Key Fact

The suitors are killed by Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius in Book 22. Homer frames the slaughter as divinely sanctioned justice: the suitors violated xenia, threatened the rightful king’s household, and dishonoured the gods. Athena’s presence in the hall confirms divine approval.

The scale of the killing in Book 22 — over a hundred young noblemen murdered in the great hall — can shock modern readers. Homer is not naive about this: the families of the suitors object in Book 24 and Odysseus faces a further threat of civil war. Yet throughout the poem Homer has built a careful moral case. The suitors were repeatedly warned. The gods disapproved. Odysseus returned precisely in time to prevent Penelope being forced into a new marriage. The contest of the bow — Penelope’s idea, not Odysseus’s — gave the suitors every opportunity to redeem themselves if any had the strength to string the bow.

The poem’s final moral position is that the gods uphold justice, and that those who violate the sacred laws of xenia and respect for a rightful king will be punished. Odysseus is the instrument of that punishment. Whether readers find this satisfying or disturbing often depends on whether they share Homer’s worldview — and that difference of response is itself worth discussing in a good exam answer.
exam_tip_html: Books 19, 21 and 22 are rich with source analysis opportunities. For a ‘source analysis’ question, look for what specific details reveal: the scar passage in Book 19 reveals Odysseus’s past and uses the technique of digression to slow the pace at the crucial moment of recognition; the bow contest in Book 21 uses an extended simile (stringing the lyre) to signal Odysseus’s mastery. The biggest error students make in essay questions on the homecoming is failing to discuss what the events mean rather than what happens. Always connect the plot to a theme: recognition scenes test loyalty; the bow contest tests fitness to rule; the slaughter tests the poem’s concept of justice and xenia.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In Book 19, Odysseus (disguised) talks with Penelope and is recognised by his nurse Eurycleia through a scar on his thigh; Homer uses a long digression about the scar’s origins to build tension at the moment of recognition.
  • In Book 21, Odysseus strings his own great bow with ease after all the suitors fail, signalling that the reckoning has come; the bow contest was devised by Penelope, not Odysseus, paralleling her husband’s own cunning.
  • In Book 22, Odysseus kills all the suitors with the help of Telemachus and two loyal servants; Homer frames this as divinely sanctioned justice against those who violated xenia and dishonoured a rightful king.

practice_questions.text: Name the loyal nurse who recognises Odysseus by his scar in Book 19.
Describe Penelope's weaving trick and explain what it reveals about her character.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: she weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unpicks it each night. 1 mark for: this delays her from having to choose a husband among the suitors. 1 mark for a character point: it shows she is resourceful / intelligent / loyal to Odysseus — a mirror of his own cunning (accept any well-expressed character observation).

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of a moment from Book 21 of the Odyssey:

'The suitors tried one by one to string the great bow, but none could bend it. Then the beggar asked to be allowed to try. The suitors laughed and refused, but Penelope insisted he be given the chance. He took the bow, turned it this way and that as a skilled musician examines a lyre before fitting a new string, then strung it with ease and shot the arrow clean through all twelve axes.'

What does this passage reveal about the character of Odysseus and the significance of the bow? Refer to specific details from the passage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details with developed explanation. Likely points: the suitors' laughter and refusal contrast with their failure — the ease of Odysseus's stringing is all the more dramatic for their failure; the extended simile of the lyre player — comparing stringing a weapon to the gentle skill of a musician — suggests mastery and control rather than brute force, consistent with metis as Odysseus's defining quality; Penelope insisting on his right to try shows her intelligence (she may recognise him or sense this is the right moment); the detail of 'turning it this way and that' shows confident assessment, not uncertainty. Candidates who refer to specific phrases score more highly.
Secure: Two details identified and explained.
Developing: One detail explained clearly.
Emerging: General statement about Odysseus being strong or clever with little textual reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Homer presents the killing of the suitors in Book 22 as an act of justice rather than simply an act of revenge.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the suitors violated xenia — they abused their host's hospitality for years. 1 mark for: they dishonoured Penelope and threatened Telemachus / wasted Odysseus's wealth. 1 mark for: divine sanction — Athena is present in the hall, showing the gods approve. 1 mark for: the contest of the bow gave the suitors a fair chance; their failure shows they are unfit to rule.

practice_questions.text: 'The recognition of Odysseus by Eurycleia in Book 19 is the most dramatically effective scene in the homecoming books.' How far do you agree? Refer to specific episodes from Books 19, 21 and 22 to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that considers multiple recognition and climax scenes. For Book 19 Eurycleia scene: uses long digression (the scar story) to slow pace and build tension; dramatic irony (audience knows Odysseus; Penelope does not); the silencing gesture reveals Odysseus's self-control. Against: the bow scene in Book 21 is the public revelation — Homer uses the lyre simile to make it majestic and inevitable; the slaughter in Book 22 is the most dramatic action climax, featuring divine intervention and the full reversal of fortune. Candidates who quote specific details and connect scenes to themes (recognition, justice, xenia) will score highly. Supported judgement required.
Secure: Two scenes discussed with relevant detail.
Developing: Mostly focused on one scene; limited comparison.
Emerging: Narrative account of the homecoming books with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the theme of loyalty is important in Books 19–22 of the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed examples of loyalty (and/or its contrast with disloyalty). Points could include: Eurycleia's loyalty — she recognises Odysseus and keeps his secret, enabling the plan; Eumaeus and Philoetius join the battle, contrasted with Melanthius and the twelve disloyal maidservants who side with the suitors and are punished; Penelope's twenty-year loyalty is what the whole homecoming seeks to vindicate. Each point should explain what the loyalty (or its absence) reveals about the poem's values.
Secure: Two examples with explanation.
Developing: One example developed, or two named without development.
Emerging: General mention of loyalty without specific examples.

knowledge_checks.q: How does Eurycleia recognise Odysseus in Book 19?
options: She recognises a scar on his thigh
Penelope tells her who he is

knowledge_checks.q: What contest does Penelope set in Book 21?
options: A wrestling match between the suitors
A race around the palace courtyard
Stringing Odysseus's bow and shooting through twelve axe-heads
A riddle competition to win her hand

knowledge_checks.q: Penelope delayed choosing a husband by weaving a burial shroud by day and _____ it by night.
In Book 22, Odysseus is helped to kill the suitors by Telemachus and two loyal servants: the swineherd Eumaeus and the _____ Philoetius.
Match each servant to their role in the homecoming books:
right: Loyal nurse who recognises Odysseus by his scar and keeps his secret
Loyal swineherd who fights alongside Odysseus in Book 22
Disloyal goatherd who sides with the suitors and is punished after the slaughter

flashcard_questions.q: What disguise does Athena give Odysseus when he arrives in Ithaca?
flashcard_questions.a: She transforms him into an old beggar so the suitors will not recognise him.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Penelope's weaving trick in the Odyssey?
flashcard_questions.a: She weaves a shroud by day and unpicks it each night to delay choosing a new husband.

flashcard_questions.q: In Book 19, how does Eurycleia recognise Odysseus?
flashcard_questions.a: While washing his feet, she feels a scar on his thigh from a boar hunt in his youth.

flashcard_questions.q: Who gave Odysseus the great bow before he left for Troy?
What contest does Penelope devise in Book 21?
flashcard_questions.a: String Odysseus's bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe-heads in a row.

flashcard_questions.q: What extended simile does Homer use when Odysseus strings the bow?
flashcard_questions.a: He strings it as easily as a skilled musician fits a new string to a lyre.

flashcard_questions.q: What is dike in the context of the Odyssey?
flashcard_questions.a: Justice or rightful retribution — the moral framework that sanctions Odysseus's revenge.

flashcard_questions.q: Which goddess is present in the hall during the slaughter of the suitors, confirming divine approval?
What fate befalls the twelve disloyal maidservants after the suitors are killed?
flashcard_questions.a: They are made to clean the hall then hanged in the courtyard.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the recognition of Odysseus by Eurycleia reveal about Homer's narrative technique?
flashcard_questions.a: He uses a long digression (the scar's origin) to slow the pace and build dramatic tension.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Homer frame the killing of the suitors as justice rather than murder?
flashcard_questions.a: The suitors violated xenia, dishonoured the household, and the gods — especially Athena — sanction the act.

glossary_terms.definition: Goddess of wisdom, crafts and warfare in Greek mythology; she is Odysseus's divine protector throughout the poem and frequently intervenes to help him.
Odysseus's faithful wife, who has waited twenty years for his return, keeping the suitors at bay through her own intelligence and resourcefulness.
Odysseus's aged nurse who recognises him by a scar on his thigh while washing his feet in Book 19; she was his nurse when he was a child.

From the Greek word for 'recognition'; the literary term for the pivotal moment in which a character moves from ignorance to knowledge of a person's true identity. In Book 19, the anagnorisis is the moment Eurycleia recognises Odysseus from his scar.
In the Homeric world, the satisfaction due to someone whose honour or possessions have been violated; closely connected to the idea of divine justice and retribution.
